title: A&P: Blood, Immunity, Skin & Reproduction
summary: What blood is made of and what stops it leaking, how the body defends itself and what happens when that defense is missing or overshoots, and the skin and reproductive systems that produce the can't-miss emergencies. Built around the anticoagulated head strike and the neutropenic fever.

lessons.title: What blood is made of
lessons.body:
## Five liters, two halves

An adult carries about `5 L` of blood, roughly `7–8%` of body weight. Spin it in a tube and it separates.

**Plasma**, about `55%`, is the straw-colored liquid: `92%` water plus the proteins that do work. **Albumin** holds fluid inside vessels by oncotic pressure. **Globulins** include the antibodies. **Fibrinogen** becomes the mesh of a clot. Plasma also carries electrolytes, glucose, hormones and waste. Plasma minus fibrinogen and the other clotting factors is called serum.

**Formed elements**, about `45%`, are the cells.

### Red cells and hemoglobin

A red blood cell (erythrocyte) is a biconcave disc with no nucleus and no mitochondria — it gave up both to carry more cargo and to bend through capillaries narrower than itself. It lives about `120 days` and is then broken down, mostly in the spleen.

Each red cell holds roughly `250 million` hemoglobin molecules. One hemoglobin is four globin chains (two alpha, two beta in adults), each wrapped around a heme group with an iron atom at the center. Each iron binds one oxygen molecule, so **one hemoglobin carries four oxygens**.

- Normal hemoglobin: `13.5–17.5 g/dL` in men, `12–16 g/dL` in women
- **Hematocrit** is the percentage of blood volume that is red cells: `40–52%` in men, `36–48%` in women. It runs roughly three times the hemoglobin.
- Red cell count, mean corpuscular volume (MCV, normal `80–100 fL`) and the rest of the indices describe size and count.

> **Key:** Hemoglobin measures oxygen-carrying capacity. Hematocrit measures how crowded the blood is. They track together, but a hemorrhaging patient's numbers lag behind reality because they are losing whole blood and have not yet diluted.

### White cells and the differential

Normal white count is `4,500–11,000/microliter`. The differential tells you which army showed up, and that is the diagnostic part.

| Cell | Share | Job | A high count suggests |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neutrophils | `55–70%` | eat bacteria, first responders, live hours to days | bacterial infection, stress, steroids |
| Lymphocytes | `20–40%` | B cells make antibody, T cells kill and coordinate | viral infection, some leukemias |
| Monocytes | `2–8%` | become macrophages in tissue, clean up, present antigen | chronic infection, tuberculosis |
| Eosinophils | `1–4%` | parasites and allergy | parasites, allergy, drug reaction |
| Basophils | under `1%` | release histamine and heparin | allergic and inflammatory states |

**Bands** are immature neutrophils. When the marrow is emptying its shelves to fight an infection, band count rises — a **left shift** — and that is a marker of serious bacterial infection even when the total white count looks unimpressive.

### Platelets

Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments shed from megakaryocytes, normal `150,000–400,000/microliter`, lifespan `8–10 days`. They are not cells and have no nucleus; they are sticky bags of granules that plug holes.

### Hematopoiesis

All of it starts from one pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell in red bone marrow — in an adult that means pelvis, sternum, ribs, vertebrae and the ends of long bones. **Erythropoietin** from the kidney drives red cell production, **thrombopoietin** from the liver drives platelets, and colony-stimulating factors drive white cells. Red cell maturation needs iron, vitamin B12 and folate.

> **On shift:** When the kidneys fail, erythropoietin fails with them. That is why chronic kidney disease patients run a hemoglobin of `9–10 g/dL` as their normal, and why that number is not a reason to panic in isolation.
keyPoints: Blood is about 55% plasma and 45% cells; plasma proteins are albumin, globulins and fibrinogen.
One hemoglobin molecule carries four oxygens; normal hemoglobin is 13.5-17.5 g/dL in men and 12-16 in women.
Hematocrit runs about three times the hemoglobin and reflects how crowded the blood is.
The white cell differential names the threat: neutrophils bacterial, lymphocytes viral, eosinophils parasites and allergy.
A left shift means immature bands are being released and points to serious bacterial infection.

checks.q: A patient has a white count of 9,200 but 18% bands. What does that mean?
choices: A left shift, suggesting serious bacterial infection despite the normal total
checks.why: Bands are immature neutrophils released when the marrow is emptying its reserves. A left shift can appear before the total white count rises, so a normal total with a high band count is a warning, not reassurance.

checks.q: How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin molecule carry?
checks.why: Hemoglobin has four globin chains, each with one heme group containing one iron atom, and each iron binds one oxygen molecule. That is the structural reason the oxygen-hemoglobin curve is sigmoid.

checks.q: Which hormone drives red cell production, and where is it made?
checks.why: Erythropoietin comes from the kidney in response to low oxygen delivery, which is why kidney failure causes anemia. Thrombopoietin drives platelets and intrinsic factor is about B12 absorption.

lessons.title: Anemia, and the one called sickle cell
lessons.body:
## Not enough oxygen-carrying capacity

Anemia is a hemoglobin below `13.5 g/dL` in men or `12 g/dL` in women. It is a finding, not a diagnosis — the useful question is always which mechanism.

There are only three mechanisms: **you are not making red cells**, **you are losing them**, or **you are destroying them**. Cell size sorts most of it out.

### Microcytic, MCV under `80 fL`

**Iron deficiency** is the most common anemia worldwide. Without iron you cannot build heme, so cells come out small and pale. In a menstruating woman it is usually menstrual loss; **in an adult man or a postmenopausal woman it is a gastrointestinal bleed until proven otherwise**. Look for low ferritin, fatigue, pica and spoon-shaped nails.

### Macrocytic, MCV above `100 fL`

**Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency** block DNA synthesis, so the cell keeps growing while it waits to divide and arrives oversized. The difference that matters: **B12 deficiency also causes neurologic damage** — numbness, ataxia, dementia — and folate does not. B12 comes from pernicious anemia (no intrinsic factor), gastric surgery, ileal disease, or a strict vegan diet. Alcohol use disorder causes both a macrocytosis and folate deficiency.

### Normocytic

**Anemia of chronic disease** is the quiet one: inflammation traps iron in storage and blunts erythropoietin, so the hemoglobin drifts to `9–11 g/dL` and stays there. **Acute blood loss** is normocytic too, because you are losing normal cells.

**Hemolytic anemia** is destruction: autoimmune, mechanical (a prosthetic valve), toxins, or inherited membrane and enzyme defects such as G6PD deficiency. The fingerprint is a high reticulocyte count (the marrow is trying), high indirect bilirubin and jaundice, high lactate dehydrogenase, and low haptoglobin.

### Sickle cell disease

A single amino acid substitution in the beta globin chain produces hemoglobin S. When oxygen tension falls, hemoglobin S polymerizes and the red cell deforms into a rigid crescent that jams capillaries and lives about `10–20 days` instead of `120`.

Triggers are anything that lowers oxygen or concentrates the cells: hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold, acidosis, stress, high altitude.

- **Vaso-occlusive crisis**: severe bone, back, chest or abdominal pain from blocked microvasculature. Treatment is hydration, oxygen if hypoxic, and prompt adequate analgesia, often opioids.
- **Acute chest syndrome**: fever, chest pain, hypoxia and a new pulmonary infiltrate. It is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease and it is an emergency, not a pneumonia to send home.
- **Functional asplenia**: repeated infarction destroys the spleen in childhood, so these patients are vulnerable to encapsulated organisms and any fever is treated as sepsis until proven otherwise.

> **Trap:** Sickle cell patients are chronically undertreated for pain because they arrive frequently, know their own doses, and look well between crises. Pain is subjective and their crises are real. Requesting a specific opioid dose is disease expertise, not drug-seeking.

### When anemia becomes an emergency

Symptoms track how fast it developed, not just the number. A chronic hemoglobin of `7 g/dL` may walk in; an acute drop to `9` from a bleed may be in shock. Watch for tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnea on minimal exertion, chest pain, syncope, and altered mental status — those mean oxygen delivery has failed.

> **On shift:** Pallor is easiest to see in the conjunctiva, the palmar creases and the nail beds, and it is far more reliable there than on facial skin.
keyPoints: Three mechanisms only: underproduction, loss, or destruction — and MCV sorts most cases.
Iron deficiency in a man or postmenopausal woman is a GI bleed until proven otherwise.
B12 and folate both cause macrocytosis, but only B12 deficiency damages nerves.
Hemolysis shows high reticulocytes, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH and low haptoglobin.
In sickle cell disease, acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death and any fever is treated as sepsis.

checks.q: A 62-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL and an MCV of 74 fL. What is the priority?
choices: Start oral iron and recheck in three months
Evaluate for a gastrointestinal source of blood loss
Transfuse two units of packed red cells
checks.why: Microcytic iron deficiency in a man has no physiologic explanation, so occult GI bleeding, including colon cancer, must be excluded. Iron alone treats the number and misses the cause. B12 deficiency is macrocytic and he is not unstable enough to require transfusion.

checks.q: A 24-year-old with sickle cell disease has fever, chest pain, an oxygen saturation of 89% and a new infiltrate. What is this?
choices: Community-acquired pneumonia to treat as an outpatient
Acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease
Pulmonary embolism, which sickle cell patients do not get
checks.why: Fever, chest pain, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in sickle cell disease define acute chest syndrome, which requires admission, oxygen, antibiotics and often transfusion. Treating it as ordinary pneumonia and discharging the patient is a fatal error.

lessons.title: Transfusion: the products, the types, the reactions
lessons.body:
## Matching blood, and what goes wrong when you do not

### ABO and Rh in plain words

Red cells carry surface markers called antigens. You make antibodies against the antigens you do **not** have, and you make them without ever being exposed — which is why an ABO mismatch reacts immediately and violently.

| Type | Antigens on cells | Antibodies in plasma | Can receive red cells from |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | A | anti-B | A, O |
| B | B | anti-A | B, O |
| AB | A and B | none | A, B, AB, O |
| O | none | anti-A and anti-B | O only |

So **O negative is the universal red cell donor** (no antigens to attack) and **AB is the universal red cell recipient**. Plasma reverses it: plasma carries the antibodies, so **AB plasma is the universal plasma donor**.

**Rh** is one more antigen, D. About `85%` of people are Rh positive. Rh-negative people do not have anti-D naturally; they make it after exposure. That matters most in pregnancy, where an Rh-negative mother can sensitize against an Rh-positive fetus and attack the next one.

### Type and screen versus crossmatch

- **Type and screen** determines ABO and Rh and screens the plasma for unexpected antibodies. Takes roughly `30–45 minutes`.
- **Crossmatch** physically mixes the patient's plasma with the specific unit to prove compatibility. Adds about `15–30 minutes`.
- **Emergency release** gives uncrossmatched O negative (or O positive for men and older women) in seconds, accepting a small risk because the patient is exsanguinating now.

### The products and when each is given

| Product | Volume | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Packed red blood cells | about `300 mL` | oxygen-carrying capacity; one unit raises hemoglobin about `1 g/dL` |
| Fresh frozen plasma | about `250 mL` | all clotting factors; used for warfarin reversal, liver disease, massive transfusion |
| Platelets | about `250 mL` apheresis | platelet count; one apheresis unit raises the count about `30,000–50,000` |
| Cryoprecipitate | about `15 mL` per unit | fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor; for fibrinogen under `150 mg/dL` and in DIC |

### Transfusion reactions

| Reaction | Timing and signs | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Febrile non-hemolytic | fever and chills within `1–6 hours`; most common | recipient antibodies against donor white cells |
| Allergic or urticarial | hives, itching, occasionally anaphylaxis | reaction to donor plasma proteins |
| Acute hemolytic | fever, flank or back pain, dark urine, hypotension, a feeling of impending doom, often within minutes | ABO-incompatible blood; almost always a clerical or identification error |
| TRALI | hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates within `6 hours`, normal filling pressures | donor antibodies injuring the pulmonary capillaries |
| TACO | dyspnea, hypertension, jugular venous distension, pulmonary edema | too much volume too fast for that heart |

> **Key:** For any suspected reaction, **stop the transfusion first**, keep the line open with normal saline through new tubing, recheck the patient identifiers against the unit, and notify the blood bank. You investigate after you stop, never before.

The difference between TRALI and TACO is pressure. TRALI is leaky lung capillaries with a normal or low blood pressure; TACO is overload with a high blood pressure and distended neck veins that improves with a diuretic.

### Massive transfusion

A massive transfusion is roughly `10 units` in 24 hours or `4 units` in one hour. Give red cells, plasma and platelets in a **1:1:1** ratio to reconstitute something like whole blood rather than diluting the clotting factors away.

Watch calcium. Stored blood is anticoagulated with citrate, citrate binds ionized calcium, and a rapidly transfused patient becomes hypocalcemic — which worsens both the coagulopathy and the cardiac contractility. Along with hypothermia and acidosis, that forms the trauma triad of death.
keyPoints: You make antibodies against the ABO antigens you lack, which is why mismatch reacts instantly.
O negative is the universal red cell donor; AB is the universal red cell recipient and AB plasma the universal plasma.
One unit of packed red cells raises hemoglobin about 1 g/dL; one apheresis platelet unit raises the count 30,000-50,000.
Any suspected reaction: stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with saline, recheck identifiers, call the blood bank.
Massive transfusion runs 1:1:1 and demands attention to calcium, temperature and acidosis.

checks.q: Ten minutes into a transfusion a patient develops fever, back pain, dark urine and a blood pressure of 82/48. What is the first action?
choices: Slow the transfusion and give acetaminophen
Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the line open with normal saline
checks.why: This is an acute hemolytic reaction from ABO-incompatible blood. Every additional milliliter worsens it, so it stops first. Antipyretics and antihistamines belong to febrile and allergic reactions, and a diuretic treats TACO, which does not cause back pain or dark urine.

checks.q: How do you distinguish TRALI from TACO?
choices: TRALI causes hypertension and distended neck veins; TACO does not
TRALI is capillary leak with a normal or low blood pressure; TACO is volume overload with hypertension and jugular distension that responds to diuresis
checks.why: Both cause hypoxia and infiltrates within hours. Filling pressures separate them: TRALI is an immune lung injury with normal or low pressures, while TACO is circulatory overload that improves with a diuretic. Diuresing TRALI does not help and can harm.

checks.q: A patient needs plasma urgently and their blood type is unknown. Which plasma is safest?
checks.why: Plasma carries antibodies, not antigens, so the universal plasma donor is the type with no anti-A or anti-B: AB. O is the universal donor for red cells, and giving O plasma would deliver both antibodies to the recipient.

lessons.title: Hemostasis, the cascade, and the drugs that block it
lessons.body:
## Stopping a leak in three acts

**1. Vascular spasm.** The injured vessel constricts immediately, narrowing the hole. Lasts minutes.

**2. The platelet plug (primary hemostasis).** Injury exposes collagen under the endothelium. Platelets stick to it using **von Willebrand factor** as glue, activate, change shape, release granule contents (ADP, thromboxane A2) that recruit more platelets, and link to each other through GP IIb/IIIa receptors. This plug is fast and fragile.

**3. The coagulation cascade (secondary hemostasis).** A chain of inactive proteins activating one another, ending in a fibrin mesh that cements the plug.

### The cascade in plain words

- The **extrinsic pathway** starts outside the vessel, with tissue factor released by damaged tissue. It is short and fast. It is measured by the **PT and INR**.
- The **intrinsic pathway** starts with contact activation inside the vessel. It is longer. It is measured by the **PTT**.
- Both converge on the **common pathway** at factor X, which makes thrombin, and thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin.

> **Key:** PT and INR watch the extrinsic pathway, which is where warfarin acts. PTT watches the intrinsic pathway, which is where heparin acts. Two tests, two drugs, and they line up.

Normal values: PT `11–13.5 seconds`, INR `0.8–1.2` untreated, PTT `25–35 seconds`. Therapeutic INR on warfarin is usually `2.0–3.0`, or `2.5–3.5` with a mechanical mitral valve.

**Fibrinolysis** is the cleanup. Plasmin digests fibrin, and the fragments it leaves are **D-dimer**. A raised D-dimer means clot has formed and been broken down somewhere — it is sensitive and not at all specific, which is why it rules out rather than rules in.

### The drugs, what each blocks, and how each is reversed

| Drug | Blocks | Monitored by | Reversal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | vitamin K dependent factors II, VII, IX, X | INR | vitamin K plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate; FFP if PCC unavailable |
| Unfractionated heparin | antithrombin acceleration against thrombin and Xa | PTT | protamine sulfate |
| Enoxaparin | mostly factor Xa | anti-Xa level | protamine, only partially effective |
| Dabigatran | thrombin directly | none routinely | idarucizumab |
| Apixaban, rivaroxaban | factor Xa | none routinely | andexanet alfa, or 4-factor PCC |
| Aspirin | cyclooxygenase, so no thromboxane A2 | none | platelet transfusion, limited benefit |
| Clopidogrel | the platelet ADP receptor | none | platelet transfusion, limited benefit |

Aspirin and clopidogrel act on the platelet, and platelets have no nucleus, so the block lasts the platelet's whole `8–10 day` life. That is why they are stopped days before surgery.

> **Trap:** An anticoagulated patient who strikes their head is an emergency even if they look completely normal and the fall looked trivial. A small venous bleed that would have tamponaded itself keeps going, and the patient deteriorates hours later. Head imaging is not optional and reversal is time-critical.

### Thrombocytopenia

| Platelet count | What it means |
|---|---|
| `150,000–400,000` | normal |
| `50,000–100,000` | bleeds with trauma or surgery |
| `20,000–50,000` | bruising, bleeding with minor injury |
| under `20,000` | risk of spontaneous bleeding |
| under `10,000` | risk of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage; usual transfusion threshold |

### DIC in one paragraph

Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the cascade firing everywhere at once, usually triggered by sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe or malignancy. Microclots consume platelets and clotting factors, so the patient clots and bleeds simultaneously — oozing from IV sites while organs infarct. Labs show low platelets, low fibrinogen, a prolonged PT and PTT, and a very high D-dimer. Treatment is aggressive treatment of the underlying cause, plus product replacement as needed.
keyPoints: Three acts: vascular spasm, platelet plug with von Willebrand factor, then the fibrin mesh of the cascade.
PT and INR watch the extrinsic pathway and warfarin; PTT watches the intrinsic pathway and heparin.
Reversals to memorize: vitamin K plus PCC for warfarin, protamine for heparin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet for factor Xa inhibitors.
Antiplatelet drugs last the platelet's 8-10 day lifespan because platelets have no nucleus.
A head strike on any anticoagulant is an emergency regardless of how well the patient looks.

checks.q: Which laboratory test monitors warfarin, and which pathway does it reflect?
choices: INR from the PT, extrinsic pathway
checks.why: Warfarin blocks the vitamin K dependent factors, and the shortest path to a measurable effect is factor VII in the extrinsic pathway, which the PT and INR measure. PTT tracks heparin, and D-dimer reflects clot breakdown, not anticoagulation.

checks.q: A patient on dabigatran has a major bleed. What is the specific reversal agent?
checks.why: Idarucizumab is the monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran specifically. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, protamine reverses heparin, and andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban and rivaroxaban.

checks.q: A septic patient is oozing from every IV site while showing mottled, dusky fingertips. Platelets 38,000, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL, D-dimer very high. What is happening?
checks.why: Clotting and bleeding at the same time with consumed platelets and fibrinogen and a very high D-dimer is DIC. Immune thrombocytopenia lowers platelets alone, hemophilia is inherited and does not consume fibrinogen, and warfarin does not drop the platelet count.

lessons.title: Clots that travel: DVT and pulmonary embolism
lessons.body:
## Three conditions, one clot

Rudolf Virchow named the three things that make blood clot where it should not, and every risk factor you will ever hear is one of them.

**Virchow's triad:**

1. **Stasis** — blood not moving. Immobility, long flights, long surgeries, casts, hospitalization, heart failure.
2. **Endothelial injury** — a damaged vessel wall. Trauma, surgery, central lines, smoking, previous clot.
3. **Hypercoagulability** — blood too ready to clot. Cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, estrogen-containing contraceptives, inherited thrombophilias such as factor V Leiden, sepsis, dehydration.

> **Key:** Ask which leg of the triad this patient sits on. A postoperative cancer patient who has been in bed for three days is on all three at once.

### Deep vein thrombosis

Most begin in the calf veins and extend proximally. The dangerous ones are in the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins, because a bigger vein holds a bigger clot.

Signs: unilateral leg swelling, warmth, redness, tenderness along the deep venous course, and a palpable cord. **Unilateral** is the operative word — bilateral swelling is usually heart, kidney or liver failure.

The classic teaching sign, Homans sign (calf pain on dorsiflexion), is unreliable and should not change your thinking.

Structured scoring, most commonly the Wells score, combines the risk factors, the physical findings and whether an alternative diagnosis is at least as likely. A low score plus a negative D-dimer effectively excludes DVT; otherwise the answer comes from compression ultrasound.

### Pulmonary embolism: the DVT that moved

A piece breaks off, travels up the inferior vena cava, through the right heart, and lodges in the pulmonary arteries. Now part of the lung is ventilated but not perfused — dead space — so gas exchange fails in that segment and the right ventricle suddenly has to pump against a much higher resistance.

Classic presentation: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia, sometimes hemoptysis, sometimes syncope. **Tachycardia and tachypnea are the most common findings, and the lungs are usually clear** — which is exactly why PE is missed. A normal lung exam in a suddenly breathless patient should raise suspicion, not lower it.

A massive PE obstructs enough of the pulmonary circulation to cause hypotension and obstructive shock, and the patient can arrest with pulseless electrical activity.

Workup uses the same logic as DVT: assess clinical probability, use D-dimer to exclude low-probability cases, and image with CT pulmonary angiography when probability is not low. The ECG is usually just sinus tachycardia; the textbook S1Q3T3 pattern appears in a minority.

> **On shift:** The sequence that should make you think PE is a patient who was fine yesterday, is suddenly breathless today, has clear lungs, a heart rate of `110`, and no other explanation. Ask about recent surgery, travel, cancer, a cast, estrogen, and previous clots.

Treatment is anticoagulation, with thrombolytics reserved for hemodynamic instability, and mechanical or surgical removal in selected cases. Prevention is the real win: early ambulation, sequential compression devices, and prophylactic anticoagulation for hospitalized patients.
keyPoints: Virchow's triad is stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability; every risk factor belongs to one of them.
DVT is unilateral leg swelling, warmth and tenderness; bilateral swelling is usually heart, kidney or liver.
PE is the DVT that moved, creating ventilated but unperfused dead space and straining the right ventricle.
Tachycardia and tachypnea with clear lungs are the most common PE findings, which is why it is missed.
D-dimer excludes low-probability cases; it is sensitive and not specific, so it never rules in.

checks.q: A 34-year-old on combined oral contraceptives returns from a 9-hour flight with a swollen, tender right calf. Which parts of Virchow's triad apply?
choices: Stasis from immobility plus hypercoagulability from estrogen
checks.why: Prolonged immobility supplies stasis and estrogen supplies hypercoagulability. There is no described vessel injury. Recognizing that two legs of the triad are present is what raises the pretest probability enough to image.

checks.q: A postoperative patient becomes suddenly breathless with a heart rate of 116, a respiratory rate of 28, an oxygen saturation of 91% and completely clear lungs. What should you suspect?
checks.why: Sudden dyspnea with tachycardia, tachypnea and a clear chest in a postoperative patient is the PE pattern. Pneumonia produces fever and focal findings, heart failure produces crackles, and pneumothorax produces absent breath sounds on one side.

lessons.title: The immune system: innate, adaptive, and overshoot
lessons.body:
## Two systems, one job

**Innate immunity** is what you were born with. It is fast, acts within minutes to hours, and responds the same way to everything. It includes the physical barriers — intact skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid at pH `1.5–3.5`, lysozyme in tears, the normal bacterial flora that occupy space — plus neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells, complement, and inflammation itself.

**Adaptive immunity** is learned. It is slow the first time, taking `7–14 days`, but it is specific and it remembers.

### Inflammation: the five signs and the mechanism

Redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor) and loss of function. Every one of those comes from three events:

1. **Vasodilation** brings more blood to the area — that is the redness and the heat.
2. **Increased capillary permeability** lets plasma and proteins leak into tissue — that is the swelling, and the pressure plus chemical mediators produce the pain.
3. **Chemotaxis** draws neutrophils and then macrophages along a chemical gradient to the site.

> **Key:** Inflammation is how you heal and how you get hurt. Localized, it walls off infection and rebuilds tissue. Systemic, the same vasodilation and capillary leak become distributive shock — that is sepsis.

### Fever

Bacterial products and cytokines (interleukin-1, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor) act on the hypothalamus, which **raises the set point**. The body then defends the new higher target: you shiver and vasoconstrict to climb toward it, which is why a febrile patient feels cold. Fever slows bacterial growth and speeds immune enzymes. Antipyretics work by lowering the set point back down, not by cooling the body directly.

### Complement

About `30` plasma proteins that cascade like the clotting system. They punch holes in bacterial membranes (the membrane attack complex), tag organisms so phagocytes grip them (opsonization), and call in more cells. Complement works for both the innate and adaptive sides.

### B cells, T cells, and antibodies

**B cells** mature in bone marrow and make **antibodies** (immunoglobulins) — Y-shaped proteins that bind one specific antigen. Five classes: **IgG** is the most abundant and the only one crossing the placenta; **IgM** is the first made in a new infection; **IgA** guards mucous membranes and breast milk; **IgE** drives allergy and parasite defense; **IgD** sits on B cell surfaces.

**T cells** mature in the thymus. Helper T cells (CD4) coordinate everyone else; cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill virus-infected and tumor cells directly.

**Memory** is the whole point. After an exposure, memory B and T cells persist. A second exposure produces a response that is faster, larger and mostly IgG rather than IgM. Vaccines create that memory without the disease.

- **Active immunity**: your own immune system makes the response — infection or vaccination. Slow to build, long-lasting.
- **Passive immunity**: you receive someone else's finished antibodies — maternal IgG across the placenta, breast milk, immune globulin, antivenom, RhoGAM. Immediate and temporary, weeks to months.

### When the immune system overshoots: four hypersensitivity types

| Type | Mechanism | Timing | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| I, immediate | IgE on mast cells releases **histamine** | seconds to minutes | anaphylaxis, allergic asthma, hay fever |
| II, cytotoxic | IgG or IgM attacks antigens on the body's own cells | hours to days | acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, Goodpasture syndrome, immune thrombocytopenia |
| III, immune complex | antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissue and inflame it | days | serum sickness, systemic lupus erythematosus, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis |
| IV, delayed cell-mediated | T cells, no antibody involved | `48–72 hours` | contact dermatitis from poison ivy or nickel, the tuberculin skin test, transplant rejection |

**Autoimmune disease** is the immune system failing to recognize self: rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, Graves disease. Treatment is usually **immunosuppression**, which trades autoimmunity for infection risk — and that trade is what makes these patients fragile in an emergency department.
keyPoints: Innate is fast and generic; adaptive takes 7-14 days the first time but is specific and remembers.
The five signs of inflammation all come from vasodilation, capillary permeability and chemotaxis.
Fever is a raised hypothalamic set point, which is why the patient shivers on the way up.
IgM is first in a new infection, IgG is most abundant and crosses the placenta, IgE drives allergy.
Four hypersensitivity types: I IgE anaphylaxis, II antibody against self cells, III immune complexes, IV delayed T cell at 48-72 hours.

checks.q: A patient develops an itchy blistering rash 60 hours after contact with poison ivy. Which hypersensitivity type is this?
checks.why: The 48-72 hour delay and the absence of antibodies mark it as type IV, mediated by T cells. Type I is immediate and IgE-driven, type II attacks cell-surface antigens, and type III deposits immune complexes over days.

checks.q: Why does a febrile patient shiver and complain of feeling cold?
choices: Cytokines raised the hypothalamic set point and the body is generating heat to reach it
Shivering is a sign of infection resolving
checks.why: Interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor raise the set point, so the current temperature now reads as too low. Shivering and vasoconstriction climb toward the new target. Antipyretics lower the set point rather than cooling directly.

checks.q: Which is an example of passive immunity?
choices: A tetanus vaccine given in the clinic
checks.why: Passive immunity means receiving finished antibodies rather than making them: maternal IgG, breast milk, immune globulin, antivenom, RhoGAM. Vaccination and infection both build active immunity, and a tuberculin test is a type IV cellular response.

lessons.title: The immunocompromised patient and sepsis
lessons.body:
## Who cannot fight, and what that changes

An immunocompromised patient does not present the way a normal patient does. **They may not mount a fever, may not form pus, may not show a rising white count, and may not localize their infection.** The absence of findings is not reassurance; it is a missing immune response.

### HIV and AIDS

HIV infects CD4 helper T cells, the coordinators of adaptive immunity, and destroys them over years. A normal CD4 count is `500–1,500 cells/microliter`. AIDS is defined by a CD4 count under `200` or an AIDS-defining opportunistic illness.

| CD4 count | What appears |
|---|---|
| above `500` | roughly normal immunity |
| `200–500` | thrush, shingles, more frequent bacterial infections |
| under `200` | Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia |
| under `100` | toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis |
| under `50` | cytomegalovirus retinitis, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex |

Modern antiretroviral therapy can drive the viral load to undetectable and restore CD4 counts, so a treated patient may be no more vulnerable than anyone else. Ask about adherence and the last CD4 count, not just the diagnosis.

### Neutropenic fever

Chemotherapy kills dividing cells, and marrow is full of them. The **absolute neutrophil count (ANC)** falls, typically `7–14 days` after a cycle.

- ANC under `1,500`: neutropenia
- ANC under `500`, or under `1,000` and falling: **severe, and the danger zone**
- ANC under `100`: profound

**Neutropenic fever is a single temperature of `38.3 C` (`101 F`), or `38.0 C` (`100.4 F`) sustained for one hour, in a patient with an ANC under `500`.** It is an oncologic emergency.

> **Key:** Without neutrophils there is no pus, no infiltrate on the chest film, no redness around the line site. A fever may be the **only** sign of an infection already in the bloodstream, and untreated it can progress to septic shock within hours.

The rule is **blood cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour** of arrival. Do not wait for a source, a white count, or imaging. Every hour of delay costs survival.

### The other compromised groups

- **Transplant recipients** take lifelong immunosuppression to stop rejection. They get opportunistic infections and their rejection episodes can look exactly like infection.
- **Chronic steroids** suppress inflammation and immunity, blunt fever, and mask peritonitis. A patient on prednisone can have a perforated bowel with an almost benign abdominal exam.
- **Asplenic patients** — surgical removal, sickle cell autoinfarction, or congenital — cannot clear **encapsulated organisms**: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis. Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection can go from well to dead in under `24 hours`.
- **Diabetes, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition and age** all blunt immunity more quietly.

### Sepsis: the immune response gone systemic

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. The same mediators that would wall off a local infection are released body-wide: vasodilation drops systemic vascular resistance, capillary leak empties the vascular space, microthrombi plug capillaries, and tissue stops receiving oxygen. **Septic shock** is sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and a lactate above `2 mmol/L` despite adequate fluid.

Signs to catch early: fever or **hypothermia**, heart rate over `90`, respiratory rate over `20`, altered mental status, low urine output, a rising lactate, and a widening pulse pressure with warm skin early that turns cold and mottled late.

> **On shift:** Hypothermia in a septic patient is a worse sign than fever, not a milder one. So is a normal white count with a high band count. And in the elderly, confusion may be the only sepsis presentation you get.

The bundle is blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics early, `30 mL/kg` of crystalloid for hypotension or a lactate of `4 mmol/L` or more, a repeat lactate, and vasopressors for pressure that does not respond.
keyPoints: Immunocompromised patients may not make fever, pus, infiltrates or a high white count — absence of findings is not reassurance.
AIDS is a CD4 under 200; Pneumocystis appears there, cryptococcus under 100, CMV retinitis under 50.
Neutropenic fever is 38.3 C once, or 38.0 C for an hour, with an ANC under 500 — cultures then antibiotics within one hour.
Asplenic patients cannot clear encapsulated organisms and can die of pneumococcus within 24 hours.
Sepsis is systemic vasodilation and capillary leak; hypothermia and confusion are ominous, not mild.

checks.q: A patient 10 days out from chemotherapy has a temperature of 38.4 C, an ANC of 320, clear lungs and no obvious source. What is the priority?
choices: Find the source with imaging before starting antibiotics
Draw blood cultures and give broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour
Give acetaminophen and recheck in four hours
Wait for the white count to rise before treating
checks.why: Neutropenic fever is defined by the temperature plus the ANC, and no source is required. Without neutrophils there is no pus or infiltrate to find, so searching first wastes the hour that determines survival.

checks.q: Why is a normal chest radiograph unhelpful in a severely neutropenic patient with fever?
choices: Pulmonary infiltrates are formed largely by neutrophils, so without them the film can look normal despite pneumonia
Chest radiographs cannot show infection at all
checks.why: The visible infiltrate is inflammatory exudate built by neutrophils. With an ANC under 500 that exudate does not form, so the film lags the disease. The same logic explains the absence of pus and redness.

checks.q: Which finding in a septic patient is the most concerning?
choices: A temperature of 35.2 C with confusion
checks.why: Hypothermia in sepsis reflects a failing response and carries higher mortality than fever. Confusion may be the only presentation in an older adult. Fever, a modestly high white count and mild tachycardia are expected findings.

lessons.title: Infection: the bugs and what they answer to
lessons.body:
## Four kinds of invader

| Type | What it is | Treated with |
|---|---|---|
| **Bacteria** | free-living single cells with their own machinery | antibiotics |
| **Viruses** | genetic material in a coat; they hijack your cells to reproduce | antivirals, and only a few have any; mostly supportive care |
| **Fungi** | yeasts and molds; mostly opportunists | antifungals |
| **Parasites** | protozoa and worms | antiparasitics |

> **Trap:** Antibiotics do nothing to a virus. Prescribing them for viral bronchitis or a cold breeds resistance, causes C. difficile, and treats the prescriber's discomfort rather than the patient.

### What the Gram stain tells you

A dye is applied, then a decolorizer. **Gram-positive** organisms have a thick peptidoglycan wall that traps the dye and they appear **purple**. **Gram-negative** organisms have a thin wall with an outer lipid membrane that releases the dye and take a red counterstain, appearing **pink**.

That outer membrane is why gram-negatives resist many antibiotics, and it carries **endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide)**, the molecule that triggers the massive inflammatory cascade of gram-negative sepsis.

Shape adds the second half: cocci are round, bacilli are rods. Cocci in clusters suggest staphylococcus; cocci in chains suggest streptococcus.

### The organisms you will hear named every shift

- **Staphylococcus aureus** — gram-positive clusters, lives on skin and in the nose. Skin and soft tissue infections, abscesses, endocarditis, line infections. **MRSA** is the methicillin-resistant strain, treated with vancomycin.
- **Streptococcus pyogenes** (group A strep) — strep throat, cellulitis, scarlet fever, necrotizing fasciitis.
- **Streptococcus pneumoniae** — the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia and of bacterial meningitis in adults. Encapsulated, so asplenic patients are at extreme risk.
- **Escherichia coli** — gram-negative rod from the gut. Most urinary tract infections, plus intra-abdominal infection and gram-negative sepsis.
- **Klebsiella pneumoniae** — gram-negative, hospital-acquired pneumonia and urinary infection, increasingly resistant.
- **Pseudomonas aeruginosa** — gram-negative, thrives on wet surfaces, ventilators, burns and cystic fibrosis lungs. Intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics.
- **Enterococcus** — gut flora; **VRE** is the vancomycin-resistant form and a contact-precaution organism.
- **Clostridioides difficile** — spore-forming; overgrows after antibiotics wipe out normal colonic flora and causes profuse watery diarrhea and colitis. **Alcohol gel does not kill the spores — soap and water and gloves are required.**
- **Neisseria meningitidis** — meningococcal meningitis and meningococcemia with a petechial or purpuric rash; close contacts need prophylaxis.
- **Influenza, RSV, SARS-CoV-2** — respiratory viruses. RSV is the big one in infants; influenza has antivirals that help most within `48 hours` of onset.

### Colonization versus infection

**Colonization** means the organism is present and causing nothing. **Infection** means it is causing tissue damage and a host response. A patient with MRSA in the nose or bacteria in the urine without symptoms is colonized, and treating that colonization usually causes harm rather than benefit.

### Resistance and stewardship

Bacteria acquire resistance through mutation and by trading genes on plasmids. Every antibiotic exposure selects for the organisms that survive it. Antibiotic stewardship means the right drug, the narrowest effective spectrum, the right dose, and the shortest effective duration — plus de-escalation once cultures return.

> **On shift:** Hand hygiene remains the single highest-impact infection control measure there is. Alcohol gel for most things, soap and water for C. difficile and for visibly soiled hands.
keyPoints: Bacteria answer to antibiotics, viruses mostly do not; prescribing for viral illness breeds resistance and C. difficile.
Gram-positive is purple with a thick wall; gram-negative is pink with an outer membrane carrying endotoxin.
Staph aureus clusters and lives on skin; strep chains; E. coli is the usual urinary pathogen.
C. difficile spores survive alcohol gel — soap, water and gloves are required.
Colonization is presence without damage, and treating it usually harms more than it helps.

checks.q: Why does gram-negative sepsis produce such a dramatic inflammatory response?
choices: Their outer membrane carries endotoxin, which triggers a massive cytokine cascade
They are always resistant to antibiotics
They produce more exotoxin than gram-positives
checks.why: Lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane is a potent trigger of interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor release. The same outer membrane also explains their resistance to several antibiotic classes, but the endotoxin drives the shock.

checks.q: A patient on antibiotics develops profuse watery diarrhea and tests positive for C. difficile. What hand hygiene is required?
choices: Soap and water with gloves, because alcohol does not kill the spores
checks.why: C. difficile forms spores that alcohol cannot destroy. Mechanical removal by soap and water plus contact precautions is required. Relying on gel is how the organism spreads through a unit.

lessons.title: Skin: healing, burns, pressure, and the rashes that matter
lessons.body:
## The largest organ, and the only one you can see failing

Three layers:

- **Epidermis** — avascular, renews about every `28 days`, contains the keratin that waterproofs you and the melanocytes that pigment you. Nutrition arrives by diffusion from below.
- **Dermis** — the working layer: collagen for strength, elastin for recoil, blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands and hair follicles. Injury here bleeds and hurts.
- **Hypodermis (subcutaneous)** — fat for insulation, cushioning and energy, anchoring skin to muscle and bone.

Jobs: barrier against organisms and water loss, temperature regulation by sweating and vasodilation or vasoconstriction, sensation, vitamin D synthesis, and immune surveillance.

### Wound healing in four overlapping phases

1. **Hemostasis** — minutes. Vasoconstriction, platelet plug, fibrin.
2. **Inflammation** — days `1–4`. Neutrophils clear debris, then macrophages take over and orchestrate repair. Redness and swelling here are normal, not infection.
3. **Proliferation** — days `4–21`. Fibroblasts lay down collagen, new capillaries grow in (angiogenesis), and epithelium creeps across the surface.
4. **Remodeling** — `21 days` to `1–2 years`. Collagen reorganizes. Scar tissue reaches only about `80%` of original tensile strength, ever.

What delays healing: poor perfusion, diabetes, smoking, infection, malnutrition and low protein, steroids and other immunosuppressants, repeated pressure or motion, and age.

**Primary intention** closes clean edges immediately with sutures or staples. **Secondary intention** leaves a contaminated or tissue-deficient wound open to granulate in from the base, which is slower with more scar. **Tertiary (delayed primary) intention** leaves it open a few days, then closes it once contamination is controlled.

### Burn depth, by layer

| Depth | Layers involved | Appearance and sensation |
|---|---|---|
| Superficial (first degree) | epidermis | red, dry, painful, no blisters; heals in `3–6 days` |
| Superficial partial thickness | epidermis and upper dermis | moist, blistered, blanches, very painful; heals in `1–3 weeks` |
| Deep partial thickness | into deeper dermis | mottled, sluggish blanching, less sensate |
| Full thickness (third degree) | through dermis | white, leathery or charred, dry, **painless** because nerve endings are destroyed; requires grafting |

> **Trap:** A burn that does not hurt is worse than one that does. Painlessness means the dermal nerves are gone.

### Pressure injuries

Pressure over a bony prominence exceeds capillary filling pressure, blood stops, tissue dies. Sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, trochanters and occiput are the usual sites.

| Stage | Findings |
|---|---|
| 1 | intact skin with non-blanchable redness |
| 2 | partial thickness loss, shallow open ulcer or intact serum-filled blister |
| 3 | full thickness loss, fat visible, no bone, tendon or muscle exposed |
| 4 | full thickness loss with exposed bone, tendon or muscle |
| Unstageable | base obscured by slough or eschar, so depth cannot be judged |
| Deep tissue injury | intact or blistered skin with a persistent deep purple or maroon discoloration |

Prevention is nursing work and it is the whole game: reposition at least every `2 hours`, float the heels off the bed entirely, keep skin clean and dry because moisture macerates, redistribute pressure with the right surface, and feed the patient enough protein to build tissue.

### Skin and soft tissue infection

- **Cellulitis**: spreading redness, warmth, swelling and tenderness with no drainable collection. Antibiotics.
- **Abscess**: a walled-off pocket of pus, fluctuant on exam. It needs drainage; antibiotics alone will not cure it.
- **Necrotizing fasciitis**: infection racing along the fascial planes. Warning signs are **pain out of proportion to the visible findings**, rapid progression over hours, systemic toxicity, skin anesthesia, dusky or bullous skin, and **crepitus** from gas in the tissue. It is a surgical emergency and mortality is high with delay.

### The rashes worth recognizing on sight

- **Petechiae and purpura**: tiny or larger non-blanching spots meaning blood outside vessels. Non-blanching plus fever plus ill appearance suggests **meningococcemia** until proven otherwise.
- **Urticaria (hives)**: raised, blanching, migrating wheals; type I hypersensitivity. Watch for airway involvement.
- **Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis**: drug-triggered, painful skin that sloughs, with mucous membrane involvement. SJS affects under `10%` of body surface, TEN over `30%`. Burn-unit level care.
- **Erythema migrans**: the expanding round patch of early Lyme disease, sometimes with central clearing.
- **Shingles (herpes zoster)**: painful vesicles in a single **dermatome**, stopping at the midline. Involvement of the tip of the nose warns of eye involvement.
- **Measles**: fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots inside the cheek, then a rash spreading from the face down. Airborne precautions.
- **Scabies**: intense itching, worse at night, with burrows in web spaces, wrists and the waistline.
keyPoints: Healing runs hemostasis, inflammation (days 1-4), proliferation (days 4-21) and remodeling out to 1-2 years, ending at about 80% strength.
Full thickness burns are painless because the dermal nerves are destroyed — painlessness is bad news.
Pressure injury stages 1-4 plus unstageable and deep tissue injury; prevention is turning every 2 hours and floating heels.
An abscess needs drainage; antibiotics alone will not cure a walled-off collection.
Pain out of proportion, rapid progression and crepitus mean necrotizing fasciitis and a surgeon, now.

checks.q: A burn is white, leathery, dry and the patient reports no pain in that area. What depth is it?
choices: It cannot be determined without imaging
checks.why: Full thickness burns destroy the dermal nerve endings, so the area is painless, and the destroyed dermis appears white, leathery or charred. Partial thickness burns blister and are extremely painful because nerve endings remain exposed.

checks.q: A pressure injury has a base completely covered in yellow slough. How is it staged?
checks.why: Depth cannot be determined until the slough or eschar is removed, so it is unstageable by definition. Assigning stage 3 or 4 without seeing the base is guessing, and the wound may be deeper than it looks.

checks.q: A patient's leg redness looks mild, but he is screaming in pain, has a heart rate of 130 and you feel crackling under the skin. What is the concern?
checks.why: Pain out of proportion to visible findings plus systemic toxicity plus crepitus from gas in the tissue is necrotizing fasciitis, which needs immediate surgical debridement. Cellulitis pain matches its appearance and does not produce crepitus.

lessons.title: Reproduction: the cycle, pregnancy, and the emergencies
lessons.body:
## Anatomy first

**Male**: testes make sperm and testosterone and sit outside the body because sperm need a temperature about `2–3 C` below core. Sperm travel epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra. The prostate and seminal vesicles add fluid; the prostate wraps the urethra, which is why enlargement causes retention.

**Female**: ovaries hold the egg supply and make estrogen and progesterone. Fallopian tubes carry the egg, and **fertilization normally happens in the tube**. The uterus has an outer myometrium and an inner endometrium that is rebuilt and shed each cycle. The cervix is the gateway; the vagina is the canal.

### The menstrual cycle, about 28 days

1. **Menstrual phase**, days `1–5`: the endometrium sheds because progesterone fell.
2. **Follicular phase**, days `1–13`: FSH from the pituitary grows follicles, which make rising estrogen that rebuilds the endometrium.
3. **Ovulation**, about day `14`: an estrogen surge triggers an **LH surge**, and the follicle releases the egg.
4. **Luteal phase**, days `15–28`: the leftover follicle becomes the corpus luteum and makes **progesterone**, which holds the lining ready. No pregnancy means the corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls, and the lining sheds.

### Pregnancy

**hCG** from the implanting placenta is detectable in blood about `8–11 days` after conception and roughly doubles every `48 hours` early on. Pregnancy is counted from the last menstrual period and runs about `40 weeks` in three trimesters.

Physiologic changes that matter clinically: plasma volume rises about `40–50%` (so hemoglobin falls by dilution), cardiac output rises `30–50%`, heart rate rises `10–20` beats, blood pressure dips in the second trimester, tidal volume rises, and progesterone relaxes smooth muscle everywhere — producing reflux, constipation and urinary stasis. Pregnancy is also a hypercoagulable state, which is why VTE risk climbs.

**Ectopic pregnancy** is the can't-miss of first-trimester pain. The embryo implants outside the uterus, almost always in a fallopian tube, which cannot stretch. It presents as abdominal or pelvic pain with vaginal bleeding and a positive pregnancy test, and rupture causes catastrophic internal hemorrhage.

> **Key:** Any person of childbearing age with abdominal pain gets a pregnancy test. No exceptions, no assumptions about history.

**Preeclampsia** is new hypertension of `140/90` or higher after `20 weeks` with proteinuria or end-organ signs: headache, visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, thrombocytopenia. Progression to seizure is **eclampsia**, treated with magnesium sulfate and delivery.

**Rh sensitization**: an Rh-negative mother exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood makes anti-D that attacks the next pregnancy. **RhoGAM** prevents it, given at about `28 weeks` and after delivery, miscarriage, trauma or any bleeding event.

### The emergencies

**Testicular torsion** — the testicle twists on its cord and cuts off its own blood supply. Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, often with nausea and vomiting, a high-riding testicle with a horizontal lie, scrotal swelling, and an **absent cremasteric reflex**. Peak incidence is in adolescence. The window is roughly **6 hours** to salvage the testicle, so this goes to ultrasound and a urologist immediately, never to the back of the queue.

**Ovarian torsion** — the same mechanism in the ovary. Sudden severe unilateral lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting, often with an ovarian cyst as the lead point.

**Pelvic inflammatory disease** — ascending infection of the upper female tract, usually chlamydia or gonorrhea. Lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, discharge, fever. Untreated it causes infertility, chronic pain and ectopic pregnancy. **Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome** is its extension to the liver capsule, producing right upper quadrant pain that mimics gallbladder disease.

### Sexually transmitted infections at recognition level

Chlamydia (often silent, tested by nucleic acid amplification), gonorrhea (purulent discharge, treated alongside chlamydia), syphilis (painless chancre, then a rash including palms and soles, then latency), HIV, herpes simplex (painful grouped vesicles and ulcers), trichomonas (frothy discharge and itching), and HPV (warts, and the cervical cancer risk that vaccination prevents).

### Sexual assault care

A **SANE** (sexual assault nurse examiner) conducts the forensic examination where one is available. Evidence collection is time-sensitive and consented to piece by piece — the patient may decline any part at any time. **Chain of custody** means every specimen is sealed, labeled, and hand-signed from one person to the next, with no gaps. Care includes injury treatment, emergency contraception, and prophylaxis against chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas, hepatitis B and HIV.

> **On shift:** The support role is simple and strict. Do not let the patient wash, change, eat or drink until the examiner says so if evidence is being collected, do not discard clothing, do not ask investigative questions, and never repeat the account to anyone without a need to know. Privacy, warmth and consent at every step are the job.
keyPoints: FSH grows the follicle, an LH surge triggers ovulation about day 14, and progesterone from the corpus luteum holds the lining.
hCG appears 8-11 days after conception and doubles about every 48 hours early in pregnancy.
Any person of childbearing age with abdominal pain gets a pregnancy test — ectopic pregnancy is the can't-miss.
Testicular torsion: sudden pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, about a 6-hour salvage window.
Sexual assault care means consent at every step, no washing or discarding clothing, and unbroken chain of custody.

checks.q: A 15-year-old has 2 hours of sudden severe left scrotal pain, a high-riding left testicle and no cremasteric reflex. What is the priority?
choices: Oral antibiotics for epididymitis and a urology clinic appointment
Immediate ultrasound and urologic consultation, because the salvage window is about 6 hours
Ice, scrotal elevation and reassessment in the morning
Urinalysis first, and treat only if it shows infection
checks.why: This is testicular torsion. Salvage rates fall sharply after roughly 6 hours of ischemia, so imaging and a urologist are immediate. Epididymitis comes on gradually with fever and pyuria and preserves the cremasteric reflex.

checks.q: A 26-year-old has right lower quadrant pain and light vaginal bleeding. What is the single most important test?
checks.why: A positive pregnancy test with pain and bleeding means ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, and rupture is rapidly fatal. The other tests may be useful later but none of them change the diagnostic pathway the way hCG does.

checks.q: Which statement about chain of custody is correct?
choices: Specimens may be left at the nurses station between handoffs
Every specimen is sealed, labeled and signed from one person to the next with no gaps
Only the physician needs to sign
Chain of custody applies only if charges are filed
checks.why: An unbroken documented chain of sealed and signed transfers is what makes evidence admissible. Any unattended gap can invalidate it, and evidence is collected the same way regardless of whether the patient has decided to involve law enforcement.

cards.front: What is blood made of, by proportion?
cards.back: About 55% plasma (92% water plus albumin, globulins and fibrinogen) and about 45% formed elements. Total volume is roughly 5 L, about 7-8% of body weight.

cards.front: What is the difference between plasma and serum?
cards.back: Plasma is the liquid portion with clotting factors still in it. Serum is plasma after fibrinogen and the other clotting factors have been removed by allowing the sample to clot.

cards.front: Describe hemoglobin's structure and how much oxygen it carries.
cards.back: Four globin chains, two alpha and two beta in adults, each wrapped around a heme group with one iron atom. Each iron binds one oxygen, so one hemoglobin carries four oxygen molecules.

cards.front: What are normal hemoglobin and hematocrit values, and how do they relate?
cards.back: Hemoglobin 13.5-17.5 g/dL in men, 12-16 g/dL in women. Hematocrit 40-52% in men, 36-48% in women. Hematocrit runs roughly three times the hemoglobin.

cards.front: What does each white cell line do, and what does a high count of each suggest?
cards.back: Neutrophils 55-70% eat bacteria. Lymphocytes 20-40% are B and T cells, raised in viral illness. Monocytes 2-8% become macrophages. Eosinophils 1-4% mean parasites or allergy. Basophils under 1% release histamine.

cards.front: What is a left shift and why does it matter?
cards.back: A rise in bands, which are immature neutrophils released as the marrow empties its reserves. It signals serious bacterial infection even when the total white count of 4,500-11,000 looks normal.

cards.front: Where does hematopoiesis happen and which hormones drive each line?
cards.back: Red bone marrow in pelvis, sternum, ribs, vertebrae and long bone ends. Erythropoietin from the kidney drives red cells, thrombopoietin from the liver drives platelets, colony-stimulating factors drive white cells.

cards.front: What are the only three mechanisms of anemia?
cards.back: Underproduction, blood loss, or destruction. Cell size sorts most cases: microcytic under 80 fL, normocytic 80-100 fL, macrocytic above 100 fL.

cards.front: What does iron deficiency anemia in an adult man imply?
cards.back: A gastrointestinal bleed until proven otherwise, including colon cancer. Men have no physiologic route of iron loss, so the deficiency itself is the finding that demands a workup.

cards.front: What separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency clinically?
cards.back: Both cause macrocytic anemia with an MCV above 100 fL, but only B12 deficiency causes neurologic damage: numbness, ataxia and dementia. Treating with folate alone can correct the blood count while the nerves keep degenerating.

cards.front: What is the laboratory fingerprint of hemolysis?
cards.back: High reticulocyte count because the marrow is compensating, high indirect bilirubin with jaundice, high lactate dehydrogenase, and low haptoglobin because it is consumed binding free hemoglobin.

cards.front: What triggers sickling in sickle cell disease?
cards.back: Anything that lowers oxygen or concentrates the cells: hypoxia, dehydration, infection, cold, acidosis, stress and high altitude. Hemoglobin S polymerizes at low oxygen tension and deforms the cell.

cards.front: What is acute chest syndrome and why does it matter so much?
cards.back: Fever, chest pain, hypoxia and a new pulmonary infiltrate in sickle cell disease. It is the leading cause of death in that population and requires admission, oxygen, antibiotics and often transfusion.

cards.front: Why is any fever in a sickle cell patient treated as sepsis?
cards.back: Repeated splenic infarction leaves them functionally asplenic by childhood, so they cannot clear encapsulated organisms such as pneumococcus. Deterioration can be measured in hours.

cards.front: Why does a type O patient have antibodies against both A and B?
cards.back: You make antibodies against the ABO antigens you do not carry, without needing prior exposure. Type O has neither antigen, so it carries both anti-A and anti-B and can receive only type O red cells.

cards.front: Who is the universal donor for red cells, and who for plasma?
cards.back: O negative red cells, because they carry no A, B or D antigens to be attacked. AB plasma, because plasma carries the antibodies and AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B.

cards.front: What is the difference between a type and screen and a crossmatch?
cards.back: Type and screen determines ABO and Rh and screens for unexpected antibodies, about 30-45 minutes. Crossmatch physically mixes patient plasma with the specific unit, adding about 15-30 minutes.

cards.front: How much does one unit of packed red cells raise the hemoglobin?
cards.back: About 1 g/dL, and the hematocrit by about 3 percentage points. One apheresis platelet unit raises the platelet count by roughly 30,000-50,000.

cards.front: When is each blood product given?
cards.back: Packed red cells for oxygen-carrying capacity. Fresh frozen plasma for clotting factor replacement. Platelets for thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen under 150 mg/dL, including DIC.

cards.front: What is the first action for any suspected transfusion reaction?
cards.back: Stop the transfusion. Then keep the line open with normal saline through new tubing, recheck patient identifiers against the unit, and notify the blood bank. Investigation comes after stopping, never before.

cards.front: How do you tell an acute hemolytic reaction from a febrile non-hemolytic one?
cards.back: Hemolytic starts within minutes with fever, flank or back pain, dark urine, hypotension and a sense of impending doom; it is an ABO error. Febrile non-hemolytic is fever and chills alone within 1-6 hours and is the most common reaction.

cards.front: What is the massive transfusion ratio and which electrolyte must be watched?
cards.back: Red cells, plasma and platelets 1:1:1, defined as about 10 units in 24 hours or 4 units in 1 hour. Watch ionized calcium: stored blood citrate binds it, worsening both coagulopathy and cardiac contractility.

cards.front: What are the three acts of hemostasis?
cards.back: Vascular spasm within seconds, the platelet plug using von Willebrand factor as glue, and the coagulation cascade laying a fibrin mesh that cements the plug.

cards.front: Which laboratory test tracks which coagulation pathway and which drug?
cards.back: PT and INR track the extrinsic pathway and warfarin. PTT tracks the intrinsic pathway and unfractionated heparin. Both pathways converge on factor X, thrombin and fibrin.

cards.front: What are the normal PT, INR and PTT values, and the therapeutic INR on warfarin?
cards.back: PT 11-13.5 seconds, INR 0.8-1.2 untreated, PTT 25-35 seconds. Therapeutic INR on warfarin is usually 2.0-3.0, or 2.5-3.5 with a mechanical mitral valve.

cards.front: What is D-dimer and what can it actually tell you?
cards.back: A fibrin degradation fragment left behind when plasmin digests a clot. It is sensitive and not specific, so a negative result helps exclude thrombosis in low-probability patients but a positive result never confirms it.

cards.front: What does warfarin block and how is it reversed?
cards.back: It blocks the vitamin K dependent factors II, VII, IX and X, monitored by INR. Reversal is vitamin K plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, with fresh frozen plasma if PCC is unavailable.

cards.front: Name the reversal agent for heparin, dabigatran, and the factor Xa inhibitors.
cards.back: Protamine sulfate for unfractionated heparin and partially for enoxaparin. Idarucizumab for dabigatran. Andexanet alfa, or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate, for apixaban and rivaroxaban.

cards.front: Why do aspirin and clopidogrel have such long-lasting effects?
cards.back: They irreversibly block platelet cyclooxygenase and the ADP receptor, and platelets have no nucleus to make new protein. The effect lasts the platelet's entire 8-10 day lifespan, which is why they are stopped days before surgery.

cards.front: At what platelet counts does bleeding risk change?
cards.back: Normal 150,000-400,000. Bleeds with trauma or surgery at 50,000-100,000. Bruising and minor bleeding at 20,000-50,000. Spontaneous bleeding under 20,000. Intracranial hemorrhage risk and the usual transfusion threshold under 10,000.

cards.front: What is DIC and what do its labs show?
cards.back: The cascade firing everywhere at once, usually from sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe or malignancy, so the patient clots and bleeds at the same time. Labs: low platelets, low fibrinogen, prolonged PT and PTT, very high D-dimer.

cards.front: What is Virchow's triad?
cards.back: Stasis (immobility, long flights, surgery, casts), endothelial injury (trauma, surgery, lines, smoking), and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, factor V Leiden, sepsis). Every VTE risk factor belongs to one of the three.

cards.front: What does a DVT look like, and why does unilateral matter?
cards.back: Unilateral leg swelling, warmth, redness, tenderness along the deep venous course, sometimes a palpable cord. Bilateral swelling usually means heart, kidney or liver failure instead.

cards.front: What does a pulmonary embolism do to the lung and the right heart?
cards.back: It creates ventilated but unperfused dead space so gas exchange fails in that segment, and it abruptly raises pulmonary vascular resistance so the right ventricle must pump against a much higher load.

cards.front: What are the most common findings in pulmonary embolism?
cards.back: Tachycardia and tachypnea with clear lungs, plus sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia. The clear lung exam is why PE is missed; the ECG is usually just sinus tachycardia.

cards.front: Why is Homans sign not useful?
cards.back: Calf pain on dorsiflexion is neither sensitive nor specific for DVT, so it should not raise or lower suspicion. Structured probability scoring plus D-dimer and compression ultrasound is what decides the question.

cards.front: How is venous thromboembolism prevented in hospitalized patients?
cards.back: Early ambulation, sequential compression devices, and prophylactic anticoagulation when not contraindicated. Prevention matters because hospitalization stacks stasis, injury and hypercoagulability at once.

cards.front: How does innate immunity differ from adaptive immunity?
cards.back: Innate is inborn, acts within minutes to hours, and responds identically to everything: barriers, neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells, complement, inflammation. Adaptive is learned, takes 7-14 days the first time, is specific, and remembers.

cards.front: What are the five signs of inflammation and the three mechanisms behind them?
cards.back: Redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. They come from vasodilation (redness and heat), increased capillary permeability (swelling and pain), and chemotaxis drawing neutrophils then macrophages to the site.

cards.front: Why does a patient shiver while their temperature is rising?
cards.back: Interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor raise the hypothalamic set point, so the current temperature now reads as too low. Shivering and vasoconstriction generate heat toward the new target.

cards.front: What does complement do?
cards.back: About 30 plasma proteins that cascade like clotting. They form the membrane attack complex to lyse bacteria, opsonize organisms so phagocytes can grip them, and recruit more immune cells.

cards.front: Name the five antibody classes and what each does.
cards.back: IgG most abundant and the only one crossing the placenta. IgM first made in a new infection. IgA guards mucous membranes and breast milk. IgE drives allergy and parasite defense. IgD sits on B cell surfaces.

cards.front: What is the difference between B cells and T cells?
cards.back: B cells mature in bone marrow and make antibodies. T cells mature in the thymus: CD4 helper cells coordinate the response, CD8 cytotoxic cells kill virus-infected and tumor cells directly.

cards.front: How do vaccines work, and what is the difference between active and passive immunity?
cards.back: Vaccines create memory B and T cells without the disease, so a real exposure gets a faster, larger, IgG-dominant response. Active immunity is made by you and lasts; passive immunity is borrowed antibody (maternal IgG, immune globulin, antivenom, RhoGAM) and fades in weeks to months.

cards.front: List the four hypersensitivity types with their mechanism and timing.
cards.back: Type I: IgE on mast cells releasing histamine, seconds to minutes, anaphylaxis. Type II: IgG or IgM against the body's own cells, hours to days. Type III: immune complexes deposited in tissue, days. Type IV: T cell mediated, 48-72 hours.

cards.front: Give a clinical example of each hypersensitivity type.
cards.back: Type I anaphylaxis and allergic asthma. Type II acute hemolytic transfusion reaction and Goodpasture syndrome. Type III serum sickness and lupus. Type IV poison ivy contact dermatitis, the tuberculin skin test and transplant rejection.

cards.front: How is AIDS defined, and what appears at each CD4 level?
cards.back: CD4 under 200 or an AIDS-defining illness; normal is 500-1,500. Under 200 Pneumocystis pneumonia, under 100 toxoplasmosis and cryptococcal meningitis, under 50 CMV retinitis and disseminated MAC.

cards.front: Define neutropenic fever.
cards.back: A single temperature of 38.3 C (101 F), or 38.0 C (100.4 F) sustained for one hour, in a patient with an absolute neutrophil count under 500. It is an oncologic emergency.

cards.front: What is the time target for antibiotics in neutropenic fever, and why is no source needed?
cards.back: Blood cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour. Without neutrophils there is no pus, no infiltrate and no redness to find, so waiting for a source wastes the hour that determines survival.

cards.front: Which organisms threaten an asplenic patient, and how fast?
cards.back: Encapsulated organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis. Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection can go from well to dead in under 24 hours.

cards.front: Why can a patient on chronic steroids have a perforated bowel with a benign abdominal exam?
cards.back: Steroids suppress the inflammatory response that produces guarding, rigidity and fever. The peritoneum is still contaminated; the signs that would announce it are pharmacologically blunted.

cards.front: Define sepsis and septic shock in mechanism terms.
cards.back: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection: systemic vasodilation, capillary leak and microthrombi. Septic shock adds persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors with a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluid.

cards.front: Which sepsis findings are more ominous than the obvious ones?
cards.back: Hypothermia rather than fever, a normal white count with a high band count, and confusion as the only presentation in an older adult. Each reflects a failing response rather than a mild one.

cards.front: How are bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites each treated?
cards.back: Bacteria with antibiotics. Viruses mostly with supportive care, since few have antivirals. Fungi with antifungals. Parasites with antiparasitics. Antibiotics do nothing at all to a virus.

cards.front: What does a Gram stain actually distinguish?
cards.back: Gram-positive organisms have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the dye and appear purple. Gram-negative organisms have a thin wall plus an outer lipid membrane, appear pink, resist more antibiotics, and carry endotoxin.

cards.front: What is endotoxin and what does it do?
cards.back: Lipopolysaccharide in the gram-negative outer membrane. Released as bacteria die, it triggers a massive release of interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor, which is the engine of gram-negative septic shock.

cards.front: Where do Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae and E. coli each cause trouble?
cards.back: Staph aureus lives on skin and in the nose: skin infections, abscesses, endocarditis, line infections; MRSA is treated with vancomycin. Strep pneumoniae causes community-acquired pneumonia and adult meningitis. E. coli causes most urinary tract infections.

cards.front: Why does C. difficile require soap and water rather than alcohol gel?
cards.back: It forms spores that alcohol cannot kill, so the organism must be mechanically removed by washing. It overgrows after antibiotics wipe out normal colonic flora, causing watery diarrhea and colitis.

cards.front: What is the difference between colonization and infection?
cards.back: Colonization is the organism present and causing nothing, such as MRSA in the nose or asymptomatic bacteria in the urine. Infection means tissue damage and a host response. Treating colonization usually causes harm.

cards.front: What does antibiotic stewardship mean in practice?
cards.back: The right drug, the narrowest effective spectrum, the correct dose, the shortest effective duration, and de-escalation once cultures return. Every exposure selects for the organisms that survive it.

cards.front: What are the three skin layers and what does each contribute?
cards.back: Epidermis: avascular, renews about every 28 days, keratin waterproofing and melanocytes. Dermis: collagen, elastin, vessels, nerves, glands and follicles. Hypodermis: fat for insulation, cushioning and anchoring.

cards.front: Name the four phases of wound healing with their timelines.
cards.back: Hemostasis in minutes, inflammation days 1-4, proliferation days 4-21 with collagen and new capillaries, and remodeling from 21 days out to 1-2 years. Scar reaches only about 80% of original tensile strength.

cards.front: What delays wound healing?
cards.back: Poor perfusion, diabetes, smoking, infection, malnutrition and low protein, steroids and other immunosuppressants, repeated pressure or motion, and advanced age.

cards.front: Distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary intention.
cards.back: Primary closes clean edges immediately with sutures or staples. Secondary leaves a contaminated or tissue-deficient wound open to granulate from the base, slower with more scar. Tertiary leaves it open a few days, then closes once contamination is controlled.

cards.front: How does burn appearance change with depth?
cards.back: Superficial: red, dry, painful, no blisters, heals in 3-6 days. Superficial partial thickness: moist, blistered, blanching, very painful, heals in 1-3 weeks. Full thickness: white, leathery or charred, dry and painless because nerves are destroyed.

cards.front: Give the pressure injury stages.
cards.back: Stage 1 intact skin with non-blanchable redness. Stage 2 partial thickness loss or a serum-filled blister. Stage 3 full thickness with visible fat. Stage 4 exposed bone, tendon or muscle. Unstageable when slough or eschar hides the base. Deep tissue injury is persistent deep purple discoloration.

cards.front: How are pressure injuries prevented?
cards.back: Reposition at least every 2 hours, float the heels completely off the bed, keep skin clean and dry because moisture macerates, use a pressure-redistributing surface, and provide adequate protein and calories.

cards.front: What distinguishes cellulitis, abscess and necrotizing fasciitis?
cards.back: Cellulitis is spreading redness with no drainable collection and responds to antibiotics. An abscess is a fluctuant pus pocket that must be drained. Necrotizing fasciitis brings pain out of proportion, rapid progression, systemic toxicity and crepitus, and needs a surgeon immediately.

cards.front: Which rashes must be recognized on sight?
cards.back: Non-blanching petechiae or purpura with fever suggests meningococcemia. Urticaria is type I hypersensitivity with airway risk. Stevens-Johnson and TEN are drug-triggered skin sloughing with mucosal involvement. Shingles follows one dermatome and stops at the midline.

cards.front: Walk through the menstrual cycle by hormone.
cards.back: FSH grows follicles that make rising estrogen, rebuilding the endometrium. An estrogen surge triggers the LH surge and ovulation around day 14. The corpus luteum then makes progesterone; when it dies, progesterone falls and the lining sheds.

cards.front: What are the key hCG facts?
cards.back: Produced by the implanting placenta, detectable in blood about 8-11 days after conception, and roughly doubling every 48 hours early in pregnancy. It is what a pregnancy test measures.

cards.front: Which physiologic changes of pregnancy affect interpretation of vital signs and labs?
cards.back: Plasma volume rises 40-50% so hemoglobin falls by dilution, cardiac output rises 30-50%, heart rate rises 10-20 beats, blood pressure dips in the second trimester, and pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state.
